claim: Measure genitives are restricted to duration and value. A mile’s walk is starred.
evidence_summary: A planning inspector evaluates an 800-metre definition of walkable and says a mile’s walk would be twice that distance. Holding the unit of comparison fixed rules out an interpretation in minutes.
finding: Spatial length is available in precisely the genitive starred on p. 470. This 2024 decision documents usage at that date. The separate proposal about weight in a pound’s carrots still needs testing.
inference: Does a measure genitive have to denote duration or value?

evidence.source: Graham Chamberlain, Planning Inspectorate (6 March 2024). Appeal decision APP/X0360/W/23/3331651.
evidence.passage: §16.3(b), p. 470, immediately after [46]. The restriction is “just temporal length or value”. The following sentence stars a mile’s walk with a spatial gloss, alongside a separate weight example.
evidence.example: “A mile’s walk would be twice that” refers to a threshold of 800 metres. The surrounding question concerns walking distances.
evidence.establishes: The length measure occurs in the exact spatial genitive marked unacceptable. A temporal paraphrase loses the explicit metre comparison.
evidence.locator: Decision p. 6, ¶27. Winnersh Parish Council packet, PDF p. 11.
